catalog_locator: Ch. 'The Moru-Mangbetu languages', sec. 2 'Tone and Stress', 2b 'Stress', print p. 31 -- the whole passage, including the closing sentence 'In both languages w…
catalog_quote: 2b. Stress. Larochette reports a tendency towards stress on the penultimate syllable of a word or phrase in MANGBETU, accompanied sometimes by extra high tone as in nɛkâ- ˈkídriɔ, headache. No such uniformity of stress pattern, however, has been found in the other Language Groups. Even such intimately closely allied languages as MORU and MA'DI have quite different stress behaviour. In MORU stress is on the first syllable of disyllabic words, even when it is a vowel Prefix, e.g. ˈiza, meat; after a consonant there is a tendency to lengthen the vowel, e.g. ˈkàˑdra, tongue, ˈkàˑrí, blood; in some few words the final syllable is virtually not pronounced: ˈlédrị or ˈlédr, person; ˈléndrị or ˈléndr, shadow. In MA'DI, however, stress is on the final vowel: iˈza, lèˈdra, aˈri, léˈndrị. In both languages words within a phrase retain their original stress.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened: Google Books page images of the Routledge reprint of Tucker & Bryan 1966, ch. 'The Moru-Mangbetu languages'), the transcript, and the archive. QUOTE: On PT37, under '2. Tone and Stress / 2b. Stress', the prose reads exactly as quoted: 'Larochette reports a tendency towards stress on the penultimate syllable.. in MANGBETU.. No such uniformity of stress pattern, however, has been found in the other Language Groups. Even such intimately closely allied languages as MORU and MA'DI have quite different stress behaviour. In MORU stress is on the first syllable of disyllabic words, even when it is a vowel Prefix, e.g. 'iza, meat; after a consonant there is a tendency to lengthen the vowel,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Moru (Miza) falls on the first syllable of disyllabic words, including when that syllable is a vowel prefix (ˈiza 'meat'); a stressed CV first syllable tends to have its vowel lengthened, and in a few words the post-tonic final syllable is reduced almost to nothing (ˈlédrị ~ ˈlédr 'person'). Stress placement is a property of the word and is kept unchanged when words are combined in phrases. (Moru is also described as having three level tones, lexical and grammatical.)
new_statements.exceptions: Statement is limited to disyllabic words; trisyllabic and longer words are not addressed. Side effects noted: vowel lengthening under stress after a consonant; near-loss of the final syllable in a few words. Contrast drawn with closely related Ma'di (final stress). No lexical exceptions listed for Moru.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms with the IAI upright stress mark before the syllable); explicitly 'words within a phrase retain their original stress', i.e. not a phrase-level phenomenon. Data are Tucker's own on Moru Miza; impressionistic 1930s-60s fieldwork on a three-tone language. Blackings & Fabb 2003:42 rejected the companion claim for Ma'di but did not comment on Moru.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's Moru material is Tucker's own field data on the Miza dialect (the standard/literary dialect; their comparative table on the same page is headed 'MORU (MIZA)', and Tucker 1940 states his Moru-Madi analysis is 'represented mostly by Moru (Miza)'). Glottolog moru1253 covers Miza, Agi, Andri, Kadiro, 'Bali'ba, Wa'di dialects; no separate glottocode issue. Note Glottolog's 'phonology' reference for moru1253, Cowan 1965 'A note on the phonemes of /Moro/', concerns Moro [mor] (Kordofanian), and Erman 1904 / Brugsch 1891 are Egyptian -- mis-assigned, not Moru.
